Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. If Bill C-42 is passed without amendment to its monopoly provisions, serious harm will be done to organizations which provide meaningful and remunerative employment for the mentally retarded who have contracted with private business to hand deliver billings, an example of such organization being N-Tec in my riding. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Murta):
That this House urge the government to provide an example and a symbol to all Canadians, in the Year of the Handicapped, by excluding groups such as N-Tec from the monopoly provisions of the bill, thereby allowing members of such groups to have a sense of worth and dignity too often denied them.

subsubtopic: POSTPONEMENT OF DEBATE ON CONSTITUTIONAL RESOLUTION-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, having regard to the government's plans to impose closure once again with respect to the constitutional debate presently before the House, and considering the fundamental importance of this debate to the future of our country, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Cariboo-Chilcotin (Mr. Greenaway):
That, in order to provide an opportunity not only for members of the House but for every Canadian to reflect soberly upon what has so far been said in the debate leading to changes in our Constitution and to free up time for the House to consider other important matters dealing with the economy, any further debate on the Constitution be postponed until such time as to allow the people of the province of Quebec to choose a new government, and to allow all Canadians to become sufficiently acquainted with all the facts connected to the proposal for constitutional reform before we arrive at a final decision.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 43. In view of the fact that the Liberal government proposed a massive increase in the provincial and municipal shares of the costs of RCMP contracts, an increase unanimously opposed by the eight attorneys general of the provinces involved, and that this increase, of over 100 per cent in some cases, represents an additional tax burden of over $2 million next year for the taxpayers of Burnaby alone, with no improved accountability, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Regina East (Mr. de Jong):
That this House condemn these massive additional costs for RCMP contract services being imposed upon eight provinces and hundreds of municipalities throughout Canada, and calls upon the government to reconsider this decision or, at the very least, to provide for a phasing in period to help the hard-pressed taxpayers of Burnaby and elsewhere absorb this further federal raid on their pocketbooks.

Several weeks ago I rose in the House to ask her about the deplorable situation of the James Bay Cree, the health situation there, and the fact that ten small children died last summer due to gastroenteritis. Last week in Mistassini a village of some 2,000 people, a medical doctor discovered ten active cases of tuberculosis and said there are probably a lot more. In response to this, the minister has decided to suspend all health services to the Cree at the end of this month. Can she explain this action to the House?

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Begin (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: PROVISION OF SERVICES TO CREE INDIAN PEOPLE OF JAMES BAY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, every fact and figure quoted by the hon. member in his question is wrong and untrue. I want to make that very clear. This is not a question that can be taken lightly. We are talking of the health and life of human beings. I would like the hon. member to be very serious and check his facts before talking about such a serious dossier.
The agreement with the James Bay Cree includes the transfer of federal health facilities and care to the Cree according to a calendar worked out with them which, by law, I must respect. According to that calendar, some transfers will be made in accordance with the continuity of the movement. They will take place before March 31. That is according to the agreement made by the Cree and I would like the hon. member to understand that. As to the health of the Cree, wherever we have the slightest responsibility, we fulfil it completely. I monitor that situation weekly.

subsubtopic: PROVISION OF SERVICES TO CREE INDIAN PEOPLE OF JAMES BAY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I got these facts from the grand chief of the Cree, Billy Diamond. He will be here to appear next week before the standing committee. I will bring him to the minister's office to give her these facts. I remind the minister that these people are Canadians. I wonder what she would do if, in her riding, ten small children had died last summer and there were ten active cases of t.b. found. Is there a double standard for the people of this country?

Second, I would like hon. members to understand the difference between real health problems and situations that we are addressing in which I asked the minister in the province of Quebec, Dr. Denis Lazure, to do his job as well to ensure that everything is all right in terms of health for the Cree Indian. subsubtopic: INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION TO CUT RED TAPE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the President of the Treasury Board. As he has been indicating for some time that he intends to introduce legislation cutting government regulations and red tape, which is vitally necessary for the improved health of the Canadian economy, when may we expect to see the introduction of such legislation which is now long overdue?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald J. Johnston (President of the Treasury Board):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board
subsubtopic: INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION TO CUT RED TAPE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the question of de-regulation and regulatory reform is not only a matter of introducing the bill. I indicated earlier to the House that we would be preparing an omnibus bill to clean up existing legislation by removing obsolete provisions and statutes, basically cleaning up matters which are non-controversial and which should have been dealt with over a period of years. That bill is being prepared.
With respect to actual regulatory reform per se, we have introduced work programs across government, and I think it was several months ago I made a report to this House on the status of that program which is moving ahead across government. I can assure the hon. member that the commitment to regulatory reform is very firm indeed. We are also, of course, awaiting the final report of the Economic Council on economic reform, which I understand should be ready sometime this spring.

subsubtopic: INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION TO CUT RED TAPE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, would the minister be good enough to give the House some sort of rough timetable so that business will know when to expect this matter to be cleared up and it may operate more effectively as a result?

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board
subsubtopic: INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION TO CUT RED TAPE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I am not sure what the hon. member means by "cleared up", because this is an ongoing process. What we are essentially trying to do is improve the regulatory process. I think we are moving on all fronts with respect to specific legislation which will, as I said, clean up the existing situation in the form of an omnibus bill. To do that, an inventory has to be made of obsolete statutes and provisions of law, which is currently under way.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subsubtopic: CANADIAN EGG MARKETING AGENCY-CONTROL OF SURPLUS PRODUCTION
speechtext:
I disagree with the hon. member's statement about boom and bust cycles because there has hardly been another product that has had more stable prices, either for the consumer or for the producer, than eggs or any of the poultry products that are under marketing boards.
1 met with the new chairman of CEMA yesterday, who is also a farmer, and with the new manager of CEMA whom they have hired, and they told me they have control of the surplus products and they will have control of production. They have made up their mind that at no time will we be importing eggs, such as was done, for instance, at Christmas time when we need more eggs for baking. Just as soon as Canagrex becomes law, we will be exporting eggs to many, many countries which, for instance, pay double the price we do in Canada. We believe there is a market there, and to supply it we feel farmers can actually increase production.
The hon. member knows that we have become so efficient that the hens are laying, on the average, 30 eggs more a year than they did before; they are living longer and laying more.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subsubtopic: CANADIAN EGG MARKETING AGENCY-CONTROL OF SURPLUS PRODUCTION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member knows full well that the National Farm Products Marketing Council, under the chairmanship of Mrs. Menzies, reports to me about once a week on what is going on in egg marketing in Canada.
There are representatives on that council from the farming sector, the consumers' sector, and the processing sector, and they make recommendations. They are concerned, as we are, about the production. Consumption is fairly stable but there is a slight overproduction. However, they have also assured me that there would be no waste of the commodity, that the commodity is being sold on world markets. But-and I want to make this clear-it is being funded by the producers who are levied 1.5 cents to put this product on world markets where it can be sold at present, where it will be some good for people in
need of this high protein, nutritious product, one of the world's cheapest forms of protein.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1981-82 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext:
That Bill C-59, an act to provide supplementary borrowing authority, be amended in clause 2
(a)	by striking out line 18 at page 1 and substituting therefor:
"eight billion dollars, as may be required"
(b)	by striking out lines 25 to 27 at page 1 and substituting the following therefor:
"expire on March 31, 1982."
He said: Madam Speaker, my motion before the House today with respect to Bill C-59 really involves two amendments. I had only intended to introduce one amendment, which was the second one, in connection with removing the government's right to extend borrowing into the next calendar year, that is, the year commencing March 31, 1982, and the amount that it might require under its budget as borrowing authority for the next fiscal year, that is, the year commencing in March next.
Since Bill C-59 was first introduced into this House two or three things have happened. As you are aware, Mr. Speaker, the debate with respect to the bill was terminated by closure. I want to outline to the House why we in this party are not prepared to go for S14 billion in further borrowing. Nor are we prepared to allow the government the opportunity to carry $3 billion worth of the borrowing authority over into another fiscal year.
The debt management of this government is probably the most inept, incompetent and unconscionably stupid of any debt management program of any government for some very considerable period of time. Only last Friday the government, in desperation, increased the interest on Canada Savings Bonds from 11.5 per cent to 13.75 per cent to stem the tide of redemptions of those bonds. At that time the government should have known that interest rates were likely to fall off. The government could observe what was happening in the American market. Indeed, on Tuesday of last week the government had foreseen that interest rates were falling off and it was able to place a half billion dollar bond issue on the public market at 13.25 per cent.
Suddenly last Friday we saw a government, desperate, worried, upset and sick, increase the interest rate on Canada Savings Bonds from 11.5 per cent to 13.75 per cent to prevent further redemptions. On Tuesday last the government had no problem marketing a half billion dollars worth of bonds at 13.25 per cent. On Thursday, when the government sold its treasury bills, it did so at a 50 basis points reduction. Clearly, if it had worked a little harder it might have even brought the

March 20, 1981
Borrowing Authority Act, 1981-82 interest rate on its debt down further. What we have seen is a government incompetent, inept and unable-demonstrably unable-to manage the public debt. If there was ever a reason for limiting the government's borrowing authority, then it is its inept performance.
The House will recall that early in January we suggested to the government that it raise the interest rate on Canada Savings Bonds to 12.5 per cent from 11.5 per cent. At that time we knew, and the government ought to have known, that it would be subject to massive redemptions of these bonds if something was not done. So what did the government do? Nothing. Since January 1 approximately $1.5 billion worth of Canada Savings Bonds were redeemed because the government chose to offer the savers of the country 11.5 per cent on their money. The government took a loss of $1.5 billion of money borrowed from the treasury which had cost a great deal to place. It cost more to place Canada Savings Bonds than any other form of borrowing.
The government watched the drain on its Canada Savings Bonds continue week after week. Finally, last Friday, in absolute desperation and shaking in their boots, the government increased the rate to 13.75 per cent. By Tuesday of this week the bond rate was 13.25 per cent. By Thursday interest rates had dropped on treasury bills even further. As a result, what has the government done? It has lost all sorts of investment in Canada by the small savers. They were not treated fairly. It is not hard to understand how frustrated anyone looking at the management of money must feel in view of the inept and incompetent debt efforts of this government.
In the committee we got into the question of the management of debt money. No less than the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) appeared before the committee. In talking about the government's total ineptness it would be improper of me if I did not read into the record an exchange between myself and the minister. 1 asked the minister:

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1981-82 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext:
That has not been determined yet, Mr. Blenkarn.
I asked the minister when he determines it. I asked him if he determines it over coffee in the morning. He jokingly said, "Well, it is not champagne at night." I asked him one more question:
1 am just wondering where the fiscal end of this country is going. You have requirements in your budget for money, you have some borrowing authority here, and you cannot tell me what you are going to borrow this month.
The minister replied:
No, we cannot tell you that today, how much and when. But do not feel that somehow things are not being attended to, because these proposals are made and approved quite quickly, very quickly.
The decisions of this government with respect to borrowing and the interest rate to be paid are made very quickly. I settle
for coffee for breakfast. The minister denied that. He said it was not even over champagne. It was probably over martinis at lunch.
Here we have a government coming to us to get a blank cheque, the right to borrow $14 billion-fourteen thousand million dollars. This is more money than this government even contemplated spending in 1969 or 1970 when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was made leader of the Liberal Party. The government wants a blank cheque. When it was asked) on March 3 what borrowing it was going to place on the public markets or elsewhere during the month of March, it did not know. The minister could have said to me, "I am sorry, I am not going to expose that intimate financial knowledge to you; it might affect the markets." But he did not say that; he did not offer that as an excuse. The fact of the matter is that the minister was being very honest with me. He did not know; he had no idea. Yet this minister asks this House to approve the borrowing of $14 billion.
The Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Bussieres) filed the report of the Bank of Canada earlier this week. Page 12 of that report reads:
From the point of view of dealing with inflation, this was an uncomfortably large deficit for the Government of Canada to have at a time when the level of economic activity relative to the economy's demonstrated capacity was as high as it then was. I am pleased that in the last budget the government recognized the need to reduce its over-all deficit in the years ahead.
We all remember the minister saying that he was going to reduce the over-all deficit in the years ahead, yet in this current fiscal year we have had supplemental estimates (A), (B) and (C). The spending estimates of the government were shot all to the devil; they did not mean a thing. It kept coming to the House for more and more money. Its final levy against the people of Canada for this current fiscal year will probably be rammed through on March 23 next. So where are we? Pious statements made by the minister to the Canadian Club and to this House will reduce the deficit and control expenditures?
It was very good that the government produced an outline of the new spending, its government expenditure plan, Part I. I looked at it and thought it was a sales program rather than a realistic outline of expenditures. I looked at some of the estimates of the government which it says will restrain expenditures. Look at what it did to the CBC, which had an estimate of $577.5 million for this fiscal year; and for next fiscal year it increases to $649.4 million, an increase of only $71.9 million. Probably this will finance CBC 2, despite the fact that Members of Parliament appeared before the CRTC to try to prevent that further expansion of government service. We can look at one department after another. Employment and immigration estimates are up $259 million. We can look at the increased spending on public archives and national museums, and all these very wonderful things, film development and the rest, which will restrain expenditures! I do not know what restraints are all about.
Last week the President of the United States spoke in this chamber and outlined a course of action he was going to take in his country. The President talked about a possible $80
March 20, 1981

billion deficit in a country ten times more profitable, on any economic base, than our country. He said that it was impossible for the American people to live with this situation any longer and he was going to slice expenses. Today the President has programs before his Congress which will slash expenses by cutting back on programs which are no longer important or absolutely necessary.
What does this government do? The minister mouths fine words, but he only gives us blue books and many spending estimates, with one supplemental after another, which demand more and more money. Eighty per cent of people surveyed by public opinion polls have described inflation as their number one problem. This week Statistics Canada says the new inflation level is 12.2 per cent, which is the highest level in years. It is much higher than it was when this government introduced wage and price controls. However, there is no effort being made by this government to come to grips with inflation. The Bank of Canada in its monetary policy, has legitimately tried to keep the growth of money supply down.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1981-82 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext: Sabotaged by the Minister of Finance.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1981-82 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext:
My friend says sabotaged by the Minister of Finance. It has been more than sabotaged by the Minister of Finance; it has been destroyed by the Minister of Finance. We must know where we are going in Canada, and this government must get onside and do something to restrain its growth and cut back on some services and give-away programs. This must be done, whether the government likes it or not.
We may want to increase our foreign aid commitments; and that may be desirable. However, if you told Canadians that they could borrow money at 13 per cent, 14 per cent or 16 per cent, but future generations of Canadians would be saddled with the interest costs of carrying that gift, I suggest that Canadians would say, as the Americans are saying, that we should get our House in order. When we have our House in order we will be able to help the Third World and people who are less well off than we are. But if our money has lost purchasing value, if our economy is shaky because of massive inflation and if we are to suffer the unsettling effect of inflation, then we will not help anyone, least of all ourselves.
The government brought down a budget on October 28 last year but, Mr. Speaker, I could not call it anything but a fairy tale budget. That is what it was.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1981-82 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext: A fairy tale budget?

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1981-82 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext:
The hon. member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans) says it was not a fairy tale. It calculated that the exchange rate of the Canadian dollar against the U.S. dollar this year would be 87 cents but it has been 82 cents, 83 cents and is now 84 cents. Perhaps it will reach 87 cents toward the end of the year and perhaps not. The budget forecast that the inflation rate would reach 10.2 per cent but at present it stands at 12.2 per cent. The budget forecast that interest costs would remain approximately the same, even though the Department
Borrowing Authority Act, 1981-82
of Finance should have known that they were escalating. It was a fairy tale budget. It projected the increase in petroleum products at about 20 per cent, but the increase in the price of fuel oil alone has already reached 36 per cent for the year. It was a fairy tale budget-a budget of Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs. I do not know who the dwarfs are over there but they are not competent, capable dwarfs and they are certainly not large in the mind. They are great at spinning yarns, however, and this budget was a yarn, not a budget. It was an effort to grab oil revenues and we know that.
Now let us look at what has happened since October 28. Mr. Speaker, the budget has been panned by every economic agency in Canada, from the Economic Council of Canada, which is the creation of this government, the Hudson Institute, the C. D. Howe Institute, the Ontario Economic Council, every major bank, the Canadian Association of Independent Businessmen, to the little fellows and the big fellows such as the Canadian Manufacturers' Association. We could understand if it had only been panned by the oil companies lobby, but when everybody panned it, that was an indication that the projections were incompetent and wrong.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) speaks about going to Alberta-or maybe it is Winnipeg-for a new round of talks to see if he can do something with this pancake. It is not working and it will not work. It is no good and yet we are being asked to give the government the authority to borrow money to put the budget through. The budget is not right and it has never been right. The requirements set out in it are not right; the spending suggestions are not right; the inflation figures are not right; the interest figures are not right; the exchange figures are not right. There is nothing right about it.
The matter can only be handled properly if Parliament acts responsibly. Parliament is the place where the government, the Crown, must come to apply for the right to levy taxes and to borrow money. The one control that this Parliament has over the incompetence and ineptitude of this government is its control over the right of the Crown to borrow money. The amount of that borrowing must be restrained.
I am not totally against borrowing, Mr. Speaker. If the purpose were to establish solid, new capital acquisitions, that would be one thing; if the object were to issue a debenture in order to build a pipeline, to build more rail track or to enclose harbours, that would be all right; if the purpose were to issue a debenture in order to build better bridges, that would be an intelligent suggestion; if the purpose were to improve the environment by building new sewage plants and so on, that would be pretty important. Anything done to improve the economy of the country would be important. But to borrow in order to pay interest-in effect, to pay off the Chargex card expenditure of last year, which is what we are doing-is not good enough.
One has only to compare the budgetary figures to see what is being done. This government claims that it will have to borrow $10.98 billion for this fiscal year. The interest on this amount was calculated at the rate in effect last fall, not today,

March 20, 1981
Borrowing Authority Act, 1981-82 and even at that it is calculated to cost $12.35 billion. Not all the interest has to be borrowed, but the interest is still in excess of the borrowing. The deficit which is forecast is $13.7 billion and the interest on that will be $12.35 billion. We are now spending more money than we receive in taxes. We must go again, and again and again, to the market to borrow the money just to pay the interest on what we have overspent in the past.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1981-82 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext: And we compete against Third World countries.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1981-82 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext:
My hon. friend says that we compete against Third World countries for money. That is how we help them; that is our foreign aid program; that is how we borrow and hand out the money. We help to raise interest rates so that anyone else who borrows has to pay the higher rate. That is how we help the Third World improve conditions.
The government must bring in the new financial program called for by the Bank of Canada in its report. New policies must be introduced that will attack inflation. We must get things in balance. We simply cannot go on this way, Mr. Speaker.
The amendment would give the government $8 billion in borrowing authority. Even with the present spending plans, that amount would carry us through until the end of October. If the government has not changed its fiscal stance by the end of next October, it will have to come back to Parliament. But if it is sensible, it will be able to reorganize its affairs and get by on $12 billion next year. That means a cut of only $3 billion, Mr. Speaker, and I do not think it would take too much effort on the part of Parliament to slash $3 billion. We could do that and the government could get by on a great deal less money than it is asking for. It hopes to have that $3 billion as a carry-over, or, if you want to put it another way, it wants the right to have more slush in the 1981-82 fiscal year.
The government does not say the $3 billion has to be carried over; it says it may carry over the $3 billion. The real essence is that the government wants the right to borrow $14 billion in 1981-1982. If the government does not use the amount, it wants to be able to carry the $3 billion over so that it does not have to come back to Parliament until perhaps June or July, 1983. But if the government wants to come back to Parliament, it figures it can, and that it would be all right to do so.
What the government is asking us to do is give it the authority to borrow $14 billion. The government's own budget has been proven incompetent in all aspects. The fairy tale budget said the government would need $11 billion. We say the government could get along with $8 billion. The government could trim its cloth, change its spending plans, and cut down on some programs without doing any serious harm to anyone. We could get along on less. We would not have to borrow as much. By doing that, we could turn this country around. We could also come to grips with inflation. But to give the government $14 billion, $3 billion more than it says it
needs for the next fiscal year with a fairy tale presentation proven wrong on every account, would be a disgrace. It is wrong. On this side we stand up and say it is wrong. We expect members on the other side to say it is wrong, but Liberal members may be embarrassed to do that on the floor of this House. They are under a terrible whip. Surely Liberals can get tough with their ministers or work something out in their caucus. Surely they have some respect for their children and their grandchildren. Surely they do not want to saddle Capada with impossible debt.

speechtext: There is no future with the Liberals.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1981-82 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext:
We were dealing with this borrowing bill in the finance committee the other day. We were pleased to have Michael Walker, director of the Fraser Institute, before us. He gave us some analysis of how borrowing affects us, our children and, indeed, our country.
The government likes saying that the borrowing is only a small percentage of GNP. The government says its borrowing is only 4.4 per cent of projected GNP, that it was 5 per cent last year and so on. If we add up the fours and the fives, we eventually get to 100 per cent. But that is not what I am talking about. When we increase borrowing, we ought to look at the increase in our GNP. If the GNP increases, then perhaps we can afford to increase our borrowing. That is another way of looking at it.
What was Canada's GNP last year? On a per person basis, our GNP slipped 3.3 per cent, perhaps 3.5 per cent. What will the GNP be this year? Will we possibly have a 1 per cent increase in our GNP? I doubt that; the forecasters doubt that. Most of them are talking of no increase in the GNP. Some say perhaps there will be a 0.1 per cent increase. We cannot justify, on the basis of increasing productivity in Canada, the increasing need to carry greater debt. That cannot be. Yet that is what this government is asking us to do.
Let us look at this in another way. How much of the real savings of Canadians is being absorbed by government debt? The Fraser Institute tells us that in the year 1970-1971 the percentage of real savings absorbed by government debt was 2.2 per cent. By comparison, in 1980-1981 real savings absorbed by government debt was 19.4 per cent. Next year it will be virtually the same. Imagine nearly 20 per cent of the savings of Canadians being absorbed by government debt. That is unconscionable.
Canada has had a great problem dealing with inflation. People are saying increased productivity is the only solution. The only way we can have increased productivity in a modern industrial society is to have more machinery and more equipment to do things more efficiently. We have to do things more efficiently to build and create. To do that one needs money. What we have with this government is massive borrowing. The Fraser Institute tells us that the government is taking very close to 50 per cent of all the debenture and bond money available in Canada. Where is the money for industry? Borrowings should not be used to pay old interest bills, nor should they be spent on current living expenses. Money should be

available for worth-while, new, hard-nosed, hard-surfaced development which will create and build on the productivity which Canadians are capable of.
This government's borrowing plans suck up the available savings of Canadians making it impossible for industry and business, and in particular small business, to borrow. These borrowing plans drive up interest rates. They drive up interest rates for home mortgages and for farmers. The government's planS are causing interest rates to be driven up right across the board, crowding out legitimate business and paying instead for bigger and bigger government. This practice must cease.
This bill must reduce the government's requirements to $8 billion this coming year. We should not allow the government to have a hangover on its borrowing authority.

I have referred to the tremendous increase in our debt. It is not by coincidence that that increase is reflected also in the spending levels of government. We must not forget that in 1975 the government increased spending by 22 per cent. In 1974, it was 28 per cent; in 1973, it was 11 per cent; in 1972, it was 15 per cent; in 1971, it was 13 per cent; in preceding years
it was 10 per cent, 11 per cent, 12 per cent and 14 per cent. Those were the increases of the late 1960s and the early 1970s.

That is the trouble we are living with. This is a government without discipline, a government without any sense of responsibility. Unfortunately, the price does not come out of the salaries of its members. They do not get a reduction for their inefficiency and their bungling. It comes out much in the form of a mortgage on this generation and future generations, who will have to live with tens of billions of dollars of needless borrowing for years to come.
Hopefully many other members plan to speak on this amendment. I will not take any longer; I hope to speak later on the bill itself. But the time has come when the House must start dealing more seriously with a government which has lost all sense of responsibility. It is a runaway government which has lost control of the Canadian economy. Let not any minister over there-certainly not the Prime Minister or the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen)- stand up and claim in the future that they do not understand why there is inflation in the country. They are the cause of inflation; they are manufacturing inflation. If there is any industry for which Ottawa should be known currently, it is the great manufacturer of inflation with which the country must live.

At page 19 of his printed budgetary statement on October 28, the Minister of Finance said the following about government borrowing:
We have been able to raise the large amount of funds we need through the sales of marketable bonds and treasury bills without hampering the Bank of Canada's ability to keep money supply growth within the target band. I am conscious of the risks we have run, however, in such a heavy reliance on borrowed money and I have referred already to the burden which it creates in the form of rapidly rising interest costs. The planned reduction in our financial requirements will be beneficial on both counts.
He predicted that financial requirements would decline more rapidly than the budgetary deficit, going from $12.2 billion in fiscal 1980-81 to $11 billion in 1981-82, to $8.4 billion in 1982-83, and to $7.2 billion in 1983-84.

There seems to be a $3 billion overrun. I know the government lives very comfortably with overruns, but that seems to be a very, very large one.
This is the reason I think my colleague's amendment to reduce the total borrowing authority is justified. Certainly it is

justified, unless we receive better evidence as to why the government needs these funds. speakerposition: Minister of State (Finance)
subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1981-82 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext:
We are all aware of the repeated support given by the hon. Minister of Finance to the policy of the Bank of Canada to reduce progressively the money supply by reducing the M-l bracket, an approach which will allow us in the long term to gain on inflationary pressures. The determination expressed in the budget papers to reduce the deficit and government spending over a certain period confirms and supports the monetary policy followed by the government bank by restraining government spending.
During a recent lecture, the Minister of Finance also mentioned an extremely important question, that is the need for a collective will to fight inflation. This will must be reflected in concrete efforts by every sector of the economy showing that they also want to reduce inflationary pressures and finally win the fight against inflation. There are many ways in which to show such a will. For instance, it is necessary to increase our productivity as a producing country, and this need does not concern only the workers. It also affects capital and investments. We need to make our business sector more productive in order to become more competitive, to set much lower prices and thus succeed in increasing our capacity not only on the domestic market, but also and mostly on foreign markets.
The budget speech of the Minister of Finance therefore outlined how the minister intended to fight against inflation, how he planned to reduce government expenditures, how he intended to reduce the government deficit over a certain period, and by setting out the financial requirements of the government, he outlined the need for borrowing authority, which resulted in the bill now under consideration that requests this $14 billion borrowing authority to balance the financial requirements of the government. During consideration of the budgetary estimates, the House had the opportunity to examine the use made of government expenditures, and I am convinced that it will now grant the government this $14 billion borrowing power.

Mr. Speaker, it would seem to me as we go along that the borrowing authority requirements go higher and higher. One reason is that there is a misleading impression given again and again in the presentation of the estimates that public spending by the Government of Canada is being kept within certain limits.
At the finance committee the other day I pointed out to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston), to the deputy governor of the Bank of Canada, and my colleagues that, as responsible writers have indicated very clearly through newspapers, in the preparation of the estimates a practice has developed of presenting them on a selective net expenditure basis. Regardless of how much is to be spent, if there are moneys coming in from another source for these expenditures, the two sums are netted and that is all that is shown as the expenditure. A classic example is unemployment insurance. We know employees and employers make contributions to that fund. Those amounts are brought in on the one hand. Then the government, because of the level of unemployment, spends perhaps $5 billion or $6 billion more on unemployment insurance, but the contributions deducted from the government contribution appear in the estimates on a net basis.
As reported in Hansard for February 26, 1981, at page 7716, the President of the Treasury Board said:
Total spending of $67.6 billion in 1981-1982 is 12.8 per cent higher than last year's level. This rate of growth, while somewhat higher than over the past few years, is below 1980-1981 growth. Total spending is forecast to increase by about 10 per cent in the two planning years beyond 1981-1982. I would stress that these increases meet the government's continuing commitment to expenditure restraint.
We know that part of the government's electoral campaign promises in 1979-1980 was to contain the growth of government expenditures to within the increase in the gross national product. This is an attempt to hide the fact that the government has failed miserably to do so. One of the principal reasons is that idiotic sort of "bread and circus furnished to the Roman mob" denial of an 18-cent increase in the price of a
gallon of gasoline. On the other hand, to charge to national revenues an additional $3.5 billion to meet the increase in the price of offshore crude so as to pay a subsidy or to subsidize increasing consumption of petroleum products in Canada at a lower price, means in itself that we live in a fool's paradise.
The public of Canada was treated with contempt by the Liberals, and the New Democratic Party who went along with it, because anyone's intelligence is boggled by the absurdity of subsidizing increasing consumption of a non-renewable resource at much lower than world prices. This is a price even lower than 75 per cent of the world price which the producing provinces were prepared to accept. I say quite frankly in examining the estimates this year that they are not $67,625 billion, they are much closer to $80 billion.
Why do we want borrowing authority for $14 billion plus the carry-over of $3 billion from the previous year? The minister was quite candid and admitted this was the practice, and it is in this bill. There is a provision for a cushion to carry-over of $3 billion. Therefore, $17 billion is the size of that cushion, if it is all spent. There is a $3 billion carry-over and $14 billion in additional authority. The parliamentary secretary looks in amazement from behind the curtain. But I tell him that is so. The minister indicated that the $3 billion carry-over was a standard practice. In paragraph 2 of Clause 1, the explanation is only as to the excess over and above the $3 billion unused authority. The clauses are the same as they were in the previous year. In essence, this bill makes available to the government $17 billion in borrowing authority this year. Again, the parliamentary secretary is shaking his head, but I ask him to read Clause 2(1). 1 will read it into the record as follows:
The Minister of Finance, with the approval of the governor in council, may, in addition to the sums now remaining unborrowed and negotiable of the loans authorized by any act of Parliament heretofore passed, borrow,-
That is up to $14 billion, in addition to that which remains unborrowed. If the practice is to have a carry-over of $3 billion, that makes $17 billion available to the government. It need not spend it all. The government hopes some miracle will happen.
Why does the government want to borrow that much? First, we are dealing with inflated figures, and second, there is the prolTlem in respect of oil prices. The government does not know whether domestic supply is going to increase sufficiently this year, let alone overcome the cutbacks imposed by the province of Alberta. Nor does it know whether there will be other substantial increases by OPEC. If that is the case, then hang on to your hat, because the size of the compensation for offshore oil will require a great deal more money. The Government of Canada will have to borrow in order to pay for it.
The government fails to recognize that the Alberta and Saskatchewan oil producers are entitled to a far more substantial price than they are getting. The domestic price for energy is artificially depressed. As the foreign price goes up, so does
March 20, 1981

the quantum of the subsidy and the government requirements are that much higher.
I know the budget provided that there shall be a levy on gasoline for the compensation account, but that is not the figure in the estimates. All that money going offshore is not an expenditure to the extent that there is money in the compensation fund. What a fine way of accounting to the people of Canada! It is for that reason the minister justifies the sort of misleading statement he made on February 25.
The government's priorities are wrong. Since October we have been involved with the question of patriating the Constitution. The question of patriation of the Constitution could have been dealt with long ago but, as we have shown in the other debate, there is a fanatical obsession on the part of one man who wants to put the provinces in their place. By devious and dubious means, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is trying to get the British Parliament to breach its responsibilities as a trustee, something not recognizable to our Prime Minister.
A much greater problem is that presented by inflation. The Bank of Canada is attempting to cope with it through its policy of high interest rates. However, it is powerless to cope with the inflation we face today; it is like a small boy trying to spit into the wind. There is far more involved in the setting of interest rates by the Bank of Canada to control the monetary supply than just the relation to that control of the interest rate. The bank cannot touch the worldwide level of increasing inflation. We have seen what it has been on the continent in the common market; 135 per cent in Israel, 300 per cent in Brazil, and equally as high in the Argentine. The Iron Curtain countries are facing this problem and we see re-evaluation of the ruble and other coinage. This is a world wide phenomena. That is one slice of inflation the Bank of Canada cannot do anything about. It cannot do anything about the increasing government expenditures, yet this is a fundamental domestic cause of inflation. The government is cheating at the federal level. Instead of $68 billion, the true expenditures amount to $80 billion. There is the same excessive spending at the provincial levels. They cover it in some ways, but it is there.
The Bank of Canada works on the M-l factor or classification which is money in circulation, money in the hands of banks and bank accounts. What about credit cards? That credit card in the pocket of each member here is the same as a bank account on which a person may write a cheque in so far as the potential demand on goods and services is concerned. They must be taken into account in determining the state of the money supply.
Cartels also have an inflationary effect on prices. There are artificial restrictions on the market supply of any commodity or service, including marketing boards, supply management and artificial quotas. There are other reasons for marketing boards and quotas, whether in foods or goods. One must remember the price that has to be paid. If the producer is to be protected, the consumer has to pay more. Those are all things that go into the inflationary spiral. It is the old bugaboo of the low-cost unit productivity in Canada. This may be the result of
Borrowing Authority Act, 1981-82 improper training in the labour force, and this applies not only to the blue collar worker but the white collar worker and, ultimately, management through lost time at work and strikes. We have an inglorious reputation over the past few years as far as strikes are concerned. Strikes and loss of production must also include absenteeism at the management level, such as the stolen, afternoon for a game of golf or stolen time for curling. It is all time and comes down to the bottom line. The unit cost of production is high.

Mr. Speaker, just so we have the facts straight before we start I should indicate that I will be voting against the bill and supporting these amendments.
In the dialogue that has taken place today between members of our party and the government, in the questions and the speeches I keep hearing the word "may"; we may borrow it; we may have $3 billion left; and if we do, we may use it in the fiscal year 1982 because there may be something that comes up that makes it awkward for the government to try to ram through another borrowing bill to carry on the governments business. That is not obstruction by the opposition parties. That is why, back when Parliament was first established, there were opposition parties to examine the King's purse and the expenditures which I am sure seemed very large to the people of the day, just as it seems unimaginable to myself and my constituents when we talk of $14 billion borrowing; not total expenditures, Mr. Speaker, but $14 billion in borrowing.
There is one point that has always bothered me since my election to this chamber, and that is with regard to financial planning, to estimates placed before committee by the government, particularly the $1 votes. When my accountant and I look at my books and we see $1 on the ledger we presume it means exactly that, the expenditure of a dollar. However, when we get into supplementary estimates, which are included, I am sure, in these "maybe" figures presented to us in the last few days, and when this bill was originally brought into the House, we also have $1 figures included in the $14 billion.
The use of $1 items by the government to accomplish a variety of things is not all bad, but some of them are outrageously bad. We have 34 $1 votes in the supplementary estimates (C) 1980-81. There are 12 votes which authorize the transfer of funds from one vote to another; five votes which authorize the payment of grants; eight votes which authorize the deletion of debts; four votes which authorize payments and guarantees; and there are five other votes for $1 which authorize reimbursement of a Wheat Board pool account, amend a previous appropriation act, increase borrowing authority and

March 20, 1981
Borrowing Authority Act, 1981-82
authorize transfer of an asset, ratify payments made in previous fiscal years and authorize an increased pension.
These $1 votes, Mr. Speaker, are actually used to circumvent Parliament. The question is: How can Parliament control government expenditures when a $1 vote is presented which represents expenditures considerably higher than $1? It takes dollars from one department and one program in a department and transfers the money that is left to a program other than that which it was originally presented for. On the transfers between $ 1 votes Parliament is asked to authorize the relocation of funds; thus we do have some control over spending but Parliament may scrutinize the reallocation of the spending priorities only between these votes.
1 would just like to give an example from Supplementary Estimates (B), 1980-81 where we had operating expenditures in the marine program to authorize the transfer of $3,989,999 from Public Works in the main estimates. We transferred that money by putting $1 in the figure when it came back to estimates.
The second way the $1 vote is used under the rules of this House is by modifications to existing appropriations, where a dollar vote is required to repeal the existing spending authority. You can see this in the 1979 supplementary estimates where a dollar was issued to cancel the authority to spend $1,350,340 in the Department of National Health and Welfare. Canadians are deceived when they look at estimates that are not a true reflection of how this government is spending taxpayers' money.
The third way of using the $1 vote is by grants and contingent spending authorities. In the case of a simple grant or contribution the $ I vote is used to specify a new recipient of funds, not the one mentioned in the previous estimates of the year. Although no new appropriation is required, the vote is needed to reallocate an unspecified purpose. In effect, the government receives a blank cheque for contingent spending authority because the vote in fact reads "not to exceed" a certain dollar value. Once we have approved a $1 vote there is no way of further examining the expenditures.
It seems to me that Parliament, having given up this authority, has lost some control over financial management and has not been able to get it back. I hear the hon. member on this side saying it is sloppy management procedures. I also heard him say some other things but I will not repeat them.

-agreement with Bombardier/MLW to purchase at a cost not exceeding $9 million the two LRC trainsets leased to Amtrak-

to indemnify and save harmless the Canadian National Railways, from any loss up to 30 million bolivars which it may incur under the terms of the bid bond guaranteed by it in support of the bid made by the Canadian consortium Canaven Limited to participate in a railroad project in Venezuela, notwithstanding that such loss may exceed the equivalent in Canadian dollars which is estimated as of January 1, 1977, at approximately $7,500,000.
By putting in $1, Mr. Speaker, the government of the day borrowed $83,386,000 for one department in one year.

This is why I believe the people of Canada are concerned and would be appreciative of the amendments made in the bill by the hon. member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) to eliminate expenditures made without scrutiny, explanation or input from the elected members who do not happen to sit on the government side.
This method is also used for amendments to non-money legislation and regulations. It is used to change the legal status of a government entity; to exempt a government entity from the application of a law; and to amend legislation without recourse to a bill. These methods are used to circumvent Parliament. These changes could be accomplished by bringing forward a bill for debate; but no, you can use a $1 item to circumvent the elected members of the House of Commons. By the use of the $1 vote in place of a bill, the government eliminates debate, it hides the workings of government from the people of Canada. In my opinion, this is probably one of the most repugnant uses of the $1 vote.
Now I should like to come to the other part of this amendment on non-money legislation and regulations. I am pleased to see the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) in the House because the example which comes to my mind is the one of a Crown corporation which was set up for $1, and this concerns the minister. All it said was:
Supplementary Estimates (D), 1976-77 TRANSPORT
A-Department-Surface Transportation Program
Vote 52d-Surface Transportation-with respect to surface transportation:
(a) to deem VIA Rail Canada Inc., a railway company incorporated pursuant
to Section 11 of the Railway Act,
I am not saying there is anything wrong with VIA Rail, and I know the minister understands this. We on this side have supported that program, although we would like to see it
March 20, 1981

operating a little more efficiently for the people of Canada and giving a little more service, as it was set up to do.
Already we have a proliferation of Crown corporations. Under this government, we continue to see more Crown corporations established. By establishing a Crown corporation for $1, as VIA Rail was established three years ago, the people of Canada, through their government, borrowed $854,111,698, or over three quarters of a billion dollars in three years. When a $1 item is used, we in the opposition find we have something over which in most instances we have no control. A $1 item is meant to circumvent elected members of Parliament. We find that although a form of parliamentary democracy has survived and can survive, the government's poor expenditure planning and changes in government policy can be effected by the use of $1 votes. There are no particular accounting practices; blank cheque expenditures or loan authorities continue to be hidden from the people of Canada in a devious way by the use of $1 votes.
When we come to the $14 billion borrowing authority, I wonder why it is necessary for the government to borrow that amount of money. It is something I do not understand. I cannot visualize that amount of money in my mind, nor can my constituents, 1 am sure. However, I should like to mention that while the government is asking for authority to borrow $14 billion, it is taking in revenues over the next three years under the National Energy Program about 49 per cent or $24 billion more than the government proposed to take in the budget of the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie).
When we see what the government will do with this money it is borrowing we find that, in its kindness and generosity, it has allocated $4 billion toward western development. I am sure the government will not have that cash on hand when it is needed, so it will have to be borrowed.
When we go through the budget papers, however, we find there only $2 billion. But I cannot find the $2 billion in new money. When you take the $300 million which western Canada now has from the Crow rate, and you add the money allocated to the Prince Rupert project, toward which this government is contributing funds under western development, and you add a few other programs, you are not even left with $1 billion; the money is in the millions.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to speak on report stage of the borrowing authority bill. I will try to answer some of the questions, as did the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Bussieres) previously, and try to expand on some of the areas which hon. members opposite have indicated they still do not understand.
The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) made a comment relating to the size of the borrowing authority. He indicated it was not $14 billion, but that in fact the government would have $17 billion at its disposal should this borrowing authority bill pass. That is incorrect, as I indicated during second reading debate. In fact, the Minister of State for Finance and the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) indicated that as well.
The confusion arises from a belief that borrowing authority will be carried forward from previous years into fiscal year 1981-82, and when that is added to the $14 billion we are now requesting it will result in a substantially larger amount. The fact of the matter is that there is no remaining borrowing authority that could be carried forward into the coming Fiscal year; there will be no non-lapsing borrowing authority available as of March 31, 1981. All previous non-lapsing borrowing authority was used up by July, 1980, when we approved the previous borrowing authority bill. The borrowing authority obtained at that point was designed to lapse as of March 31, 1981. As a result, there is no borrowing authority to carry forward into the fiscal year 1981-82. The only borrowing authority which will be available to the government is the borrowing authority now being discussed in Parliament. I urge the hon. member for Edmonton West to listen more carefully when we explain that this $14 billion is the borrowing authority which will be available to the government in 1981-82. There is no more; that is all there is. 1 hope we get that point across this time.
The difference between the $11 billion financial requirements of the government shown in the budget papers and the $14 billion we are requesting in this borrowing authority was well explained by the Minister of State for Finance earlier today. The reason we are requesting that additional $3 billion is for contingency purposes. As the hon. member for Edmonton West indicated, if world prices were to suddenly rise by 50 per cent, the impact on the oil import compensation program would be substantial. This would have to be funded, so that possibility is being included in the $3 billion for contingency purposes. In addition, part of the borrowing authority, as has been the practice-not in the last two years but in the prior
years-is designed not to lapse. It can be carried forward into coming fiscal years.
When the government came into power in February of 1980, it was faced with a problem. Parliament was called, but we could not get a borrowing authority bill through the House by the end of March, 1980. Had it not been for the fact that at that time we had some available non-lapsing borrowing authority, the government would have been effectively in a position where it could not borrow or it could not finance itself during the period between the end of March, 1980, and the time when the borrowing authority bill was passed in June or July.
We are asking for that same flexibility for our government and governments in the future. Normally we would intend to bring in a borrowing authority bill in January or February, as we have done this time, to be debated in the House for the fiscal year 1982-83, and to have this non-lapsing borrowing authority carry on as a flexible, contingent emergency measure, not to be used as is indicated by the financial requirements in the budget.
The estimates which were brought down clearly indicate the financial requirements. They will be approved by Parliament. Those are the spending authorities for the government. The borrowing authority is being requested to finance the difference between the revenues of the government and the expenditure plan, which is the financial requirement. It is quite proper and right; it is the way things have been done for many years. I expect it to be that way in the future.
The hon. member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) indicated earlier that because of the government's borrowing, it is crowding the private sector out of capital markets. All the evidence I have seen indicates that crowding out is not taking place. First, crowding out is not a very relevant concept. It assumes that the amount of available money for lending and borrowing in the economy is static, that it does not grow, that it does not expand and, as a result, if the government takes more there must be less for the business community and the business community must do with less. That is not the way in which the market system works.
In the market system there is the real rate of interest, which is the rate of interest paid, minus the inflation rate; it is the real gain people obtain from saving. If the real rate of interest goes up, then people will be induced to consume less today and save more. That expands the quantity of loanable funds. So, as the real rate of return goes up the supply of loanable funds increases. Therefore, there is a very clear test to see whether or not the federal government borrowing is crowding out-to use that phrase again, albeit improperly-or squeezing the private sector. The simple test is to look at whether or not the real rate of interest in the economy has been going up over time.
It just so happens that in the latest annual report of the Bank of Canada for 1980, which was tabled just a few days ago, we see on page 18 a diagram of the real rate of interest from the period 1970 to 1980. We find that the real rate of
March 20, 1981

interest all during that time-frame has stayed below the average real rate of interest in the period 1956 to 1970. In fact, there is no trend, as shown by this document, which would indicate an increase in the real rate of interest. If there is no increase in the real rate of interest, that implies that the volume of loanable funds in the economy is sufficient to meet the demands of both the private sector and the public sector, without putting undue pressure on that supply. As a result, the crowding out theory put forward by the hon. member for Mississauga South is totally fallacious. I would suggest he go back and do his homework again.

PARLIAMENTARY AND SENIOR PUBLIC SERVANTS' SALARIES AND ALLOWANCES
subsubtopic: PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF REMUNERATION TRIBUNAL
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of establishing a Remuneration Tribunal composed of at least three full time members who shall occupy their posts during good behaviour, and whose duties shall include the annual review and report to Parliament on remuneration, allowances of all natures, entitlements and pensions payable to ministers, senators, members of Parliament, office-holders of the Parliament, holders of office at the executive level of the public service and the equivalent holders of public offices.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I sometimes feel that there are days when the fortunes do smile upon us. Rarely can an hon. member put forward an idea contained in a notice of motion four times within the period of one year, but such has been the case. I am grateful to the fates that have allowed me to do this. Today I want to speak about something to which I adverted at length during the second reading on Bill C-34, an act to amend the salaries of judges. We looked at this in some considerable detail in the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, I was able to speak about it on another occasion earlier this year, as well as at the time of the adjournment debate last year. It is singularly apposite that we are discussing it today.
In April there were changes in some of the salaries of senior public servants. Judges have just received increased salaries as provided in Bill C-34. I accepted the level of pay with some reluctance. There did not seem to be principles contained in that bill upon which the salaries related to those of other persons in senior public service. We should be able to bring these together on some sort of rational basis.
As I have indicated before, the salaries and entitlements of deputy ministers at the executive level of the public service are based on what the cabinet considers to be acceptable as a result of the report of an advisory committee which has been known, for the past few years, as the Lambert commission, named after its chairman. There are those who hold privy council appointments through the office of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). I fail to discern any real and objective principle for determining their scale of pay and benefits. I suppose, as a rough rule of thumb, it may have some bearing on their senior executive level in the public service.
There are those people who are most underpaid in the country, starting with the Prime Minister, cabinet ministers, Members of Parliament, and senators! People may say some are overpaid, but that is a global criticism. Those who raise this question are usually jealous. That is from where the chief criticism comes. It is natural, and we expect it.
During the nearly 25 years I have been in the House of Commons, I have seen scores of cabinet ministers leave here with their health burned out due to excessive pressures of office. Not only must they do a terrific job of administration, but they must also relate to other Members of Parliament, and they must always proceed at full bore. They must also be politicians, looking at their constituencies; they are always
March 20, 1981

under the constant microscope of the people. The classic example of underpay and non-reward in this country is found in the office of the Prime Minister.

subtopic: PARLIAMENTARY AND SENIOR PUBLIC SERVANTS' SALARIES AND ALLOWANCES
subsubtopic: PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF REMUNERATION TRIBUNAL
speechtext:
It is a great honour to be Prime Minister, but, when we consider that presidents of corporations receive up to $300,000 in salary and benefits and that presidents of Crown corporations can make well in excess of $100,000, why is it that the Prime Minister gets a measly $80,000-odd? This is just a total reversal of the scale of values. That is the toughest job in the country. The amount of abuse which has to be taken by the occupant of the office is something to behold. Regardless of that, if you cannot stand the heat, get out of the kitchen. But on the other hand, he or she who levels that undeserved criticism or that blasphemous language, or what have you, is not thinking of that relationship in terms of the man who occupies that office.
Some people say, "Well, look, judges got $70,000 as of April 1, 1980, or $67,000 if they were in the county court." However, that is their sole source of income. As a lawyer, I would be the first to admit, that a corporate lawyer who earns maybe $125,000 or $150,000 before taxes might be the worst judge in the world. On the other hand, the man who makes only $45,000 or $50,000 from a small town practice could be one of the better judges because he may combine common sense with a sense of justice. He may learn how to be a good judge.
In justifying high rates of pay for lawyers, leaders of the Canadian Bar Association and other administrators of justice all too often ask how we will get the quarter million dollar man down into a court. Again, I would say that the quarter million dollar man is not necessarily the man who will be the good judge.
I was part of a large law firm, the senior earning partner of which said he would make the world's worst judge. He was the first to admit that. He would refuse to hear certain kinds of cases. He could not abide going into court to listen to what he called "domestic squabbles." He never felt comfortable with a case which involved personal injury. So the presumption cannot be made that a man who earns a big salary as a lawyer is qualified to be a judge.
1 think we should compare the relative positions of these people. More than 20 years ago when I came to this House, a parliamentary secretary earned the same salary as a county court judge. Perhaps in total the judge earned more because he was given a surrogate allowance for handling the chancery side of the court, but the basic salary was the same. As of last April, that judge would be earning $67,000 per year and in a number of provinces would be receiving surrogate fees as well. This is particularly so in Alberta where there is only one level of court and the judge's salary is $70,000. On top of that, those who do surrogate work are paid the relevant fees.
The question is, what determines that level and the size of the increase that should be given? At the moment, there is
Remuneration Tribunal
built into the Judges Act a provision for a 7 per cent per annum increase or an increase equivalent to that which pertains to industrial wages. With all due respect, industrial wages have as much relevance to the salaries of lawyers and professional people as cheese has to oranges. It is not an appropriate scale to use for comparison, nor is it appropriate that it be applied to Members of Parliament.
As my studies indicated, with a 7 per cent increase for 15 years, by 1995 the salary would be $194,000. That is mind-boggling. If we all have to face inflation on that scale, then senior citizens will draw about $500 per month in old age security, by 1995! That will not mean they will be any better off, of course.
Not long ago the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Kilgour) produced a 20 billion mark note from the old Weimar Republic, issued before the balloon went up in 1923. Imagine, a little piece of paper being worth 20 billion marks. The government does not even use that kind of figure in its inflated budgets. All these things must be brought together.
I propose that we should follow the Australian example and adapt it where need be. We should establish a remuneration review tribunal composed of three persons. In Australia such people are appointed for five years but I would suggest that in this country they be appointed "on good behaviour."
In Australia the persons involved must not be connected in any way with government; must not have served elective office for seven years; must not be part of the public service and the chairman must be a judge of a state court or one who is entitled to be appointed to a state court. The equivalent in Canada would be a provincial judge. The review board places annual announcements in the national press that it will receive representations with regard to a number of stated offices. It then hears representations and the government must appear before the board as a party. The board examines all the relevant data and in some instances representations may be passed over. The judges may appear before the board but not seek an increase for a particular year, or the government may rule that as the industrial increase in a certain year was 4 per cent the judges are entitled to the same increase. The government may also hold that certain categories should receive an increase. In any event, everything is out in the open.
The review tribunal makes its findings with regard to all the categories of persons upon whose salaries it must adjudicate. The report is tabled in Parliament and within 15 days the recommendation goes into effect unless more than 50 per cent of members of the House of Representatives and the Senate sign a motion to oppose it. When I was in Australia in 1975, that is precisely what happened. All the salary increases were deferred for one year.
In addition to salaries, the tribunal sets emoluments; for instance, such privileges as transportation for the wife or children of a Member of Parliament or a senator. Overseas travel is ruled upon by the tribunal but, strangely enough, pensions are not. In some states, the remuneration of the premier and cabinet ministers are also ruled upon.

Remuneration Tribunal
In this country this thankless task could be removed from Parliament and the public would feel that not only had justice been done for this whole category of people but that it would appear to have been done. I think that is one of the difficulties with the present system. I do not subscribe to the argument that it is morally wrong for Members of Parliament to set their own salaries. That happens all the time in the business world. In many instances, people adjudicate upon matters where one might think there would be a conflict of interest. For instance, in this House members who are farmers assist in setting the level of subsidy to be paid on a particular crop or set the price of wheat or cattle. There are other things to be determined by members as groups. We see that at all levels, the school board, the city council, the county council level or what have you. It is the nature of the beast that it has to be done. Sometimes it is a difficult thing, but I hope this proposal I have made will be accepted.
I hope a House committee will take up this matter and carry it further to see whether or not it is practical. It is practical enough for the Australians. Since 1973, when the system was implemented there, it has worked well and it has been copied in New Zealand. New Zealand now has a body dealing with high level salaries. New Zealand pretty well deals with salaries all the way through to its tribunals. New Zealand has this higher level, and I am told by parliamentarians and diplomats that the system seems to be working well and has a degree of acceptability by the population.
I commend this resolution to hon. members for further consideration. I hope that rather than just talking it out, we might be able to handle it in some way so it could be given further consideration. Maybe we can get around to doing it now. The Senate and House of Commons Act, as it provides for the salaries of members of this House-
