speechtext: I must interrupt the hon. member because he has exceeded his allotted time. The hon. member for Northumberland-Miramichi (Mr. Dionne).

subtopic: PARLIAMENTARY AND SENIOR PUBLIC SERVANTS' SALARIES AND ALLOWANCES
subsubtopic: PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF REMUNERATION TRIBUNAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to participate in this debate this afternoon. First, I want to congratulate the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) for putting this motion on the Order Paper for debate. I think it is a very worth-while motion. It is something on which we should focus as Members of Parliament. However, I have a few questions which I will outline. I am not questioning this in any critical sense, only in a positive way. The motion says, in referring to the duties of the tribunal, the following:
-shall include the annual review and report to Parliament-
But the motion does not say that Parliament would have authority to alter the motion or whether it would simply have to accept or reject it, as is the case in Australia.
The motion also lists several groups whose salaries the tribunal would review. They are as follows:
-ministers, senators. Members of Parliament, office-holders of the Parliament, holders of office at the executive level of the public service and the equivalent holders of Public Offices.
1 wonder whether the hon. member would wish to include in that category judges for whom, as he noted, this Parliament had recently granted increases in salary? He did not mention what qualifications he would like to see for members of this tribunal. For instance, would he want a member of that tribunal to be a judge? Would he want a former Member of this Parliament to sit on that tribunal? Would he ask a former member of a provincial legislature to be a member of the tribunal? Those are the kinds of questions I would like him to address. I realize, of course, those questions can be addressed in committee. I am not criticizing the motion, I am simply pointing out some of the questions I have about it.
I agree with the hon. member in his assessment that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), ministers of the Crown, members of this House, and I believe of provincial Houses-in some cases at least-are not being adequately paid for the time they put in. I know it is a difficult matter for members to talk about. Personally, I do not have a lot of difficulty with the argument of some people that we should not be increasing our own salaries. The major argument I have, which I suppose could be a bit embarrassing, is that this matter is dealt with so unexpeditiously by this Parliament. When it is dealt with, usually a fairly significant increase is granted. This makes it look as though all of a sudden Members of Parliament have become very greedy. If this matter were reviewed on an annual basis, and maybe if we had not tampered with the formula which was enacted in 1975, we might not be in a position today where we are discussing this kind of motion.
As the hon. member for Edmonton West pointed out, it would be useful to look at some of the methods used in other countries. He referred to Australia and New Zealand. As 1 understand it, the situation in Australia is pretty much the way the hon. member described it. However, I want to add to what he said, that the act in Australia contains provision for Parliament to accept or reject the actions of the commission, but not to modify them. On the other hand, in New Zealand, there is a higher salaries commission. It has declaratory powers with respect to the compensation of senior public servants, heads of Crown corporations and Members of Parliament. It also acts in an advisory capacity for judicial salaries. There is no provision for review of its actions by Parliament. In other words, it is supreme in its recommendations. Whether we would want that in Canada is something which would require a considerable amount of reflection and debate.
In the United Kingdom there is a top salaries review body which is advisory in nature to the prime minister. I would judge from that that the prime minister or the government of the day would still have to bring before parliament a bill to implement the decisions of the top salaries review body. It consists of various panels and it deals with the compensation of the senior public service, the heads of nationalized industries, the judiciary, senior military ranks, Members of Parliament- and hon. members will note that Members of Parliament are in the list of priorities-doctors and dentists of the national
March 20, 1981

health service and other ranks of the armed forces. Those are three examples of what is done in other systems with the British parliamentary system of democracy.
It might be useful for us as well to take a detailed look at what some of the provincial legislatures in the country do. I will not go into that in detail, except to say it is my understanding that in some of the provinces members of provincial legislatures are earning more in salaries and benefits than Members of Parliament at the national level. That tells us something regarding our position, vis-a-vis other levels of government in Canada. Even at the municipal level, some mayors are being paid, if not more, at least on a level equivalent to cabinet ministers and, in some cases I believe, equivalent to the Prime Minister. That situation raises some questions in my mind.
The hon. member for Edmonton West spoke also of the comparability between salaries of Members of Parliament and county court judges. He recounted that when he came here the salary of a parliamentary secretary was comparable to a county court judge. That is no longer the case. However, what I would be more concerned about is the disparity in salaries between Members of Parliament and members of the public service. I do not say that in any way to begrudge civil servants their salaries.
It strikes me as rather odd that some deputy ministers earn more than their ministers. If the figures I have are correct, the Clerk of the Privy Council earns more than the Prime Minister, as do the heads of Crown corporations. If we are to have good people to head our Crown corporations, obviously we must pay them good salaries. If we are to have good deputy ministers, the managers of our public service, we must pay them comparable to what they would earn in the private sector, or that is where they would go.
I do not suggest that a Member of Parliament should earn as much as a deputy minister. It is not that I do not think a Member of Parliament is not worth as much, but if we are to have good deputy ministers, the major managers of our public service, the business of the country, they must be well paid. If they are not well paid, they will go to private industry. We are lucky to have the calibre of people we do at the senior management level of our public service.
I believe it says something for our system when information officers in departments of government earn the equivalent salary of a Member of Parliament. That seems to be getting down fairly well in the pecking order of the various departments. If a position is at the level at which a Member of Parliament is paid, that is the level of importance that will be attached to the role of a Member of Parliament.
It is often forgotten by those who write facile commentaries about the salaries and benefits Members of Parliament receive and the role they play what the workload is and the number of hours actually worked. We constantly hear the charge that there are very few members here in the House. There are not many here right now. I am not critical of that situation on
Remuneration Tribunal
most occasions. While there may only be a relatively small number in the chamber, 80 or 100 members may be required for committees. On a Friday afternoon most members head back to their constituencies where they have to work the other two days of the week. For most members, their work week is seven days, almost every day of the year. If members were to determine the hourly rate for the number of hours they work, some would be receiving only the minimum wage. Long before I was elected, I believed that Members of Parliament should be paid a reasonable salary and that all expenses incurred in the performance of their duties should be covered from public funds. I would apply that principle to members of provincial legislatures and those serving on municipal councils.
1 would object to Members of Parliament, members of legislatures and municipal councils being paid exorbitant salaries. I do not believe anyone should become wealthy by serving in public life, but neither should he be poverty stricken. Their children should not be denied a good education and as good a life as their contemporaries. That has happened with some Members of Parliament in the past and is happening now.
In some cases widows of former Members of Parliament have suffered grievously from financial instability. There are cases of members being defeated before accumulating significant pension benefits. In fact, some accumulate no benefits at all. Some have been unable to find other employment quickly. There are employers who consider service in the Parliament of Canada a detriment to employment. That situation should not pertain because someone has served in public life.
There are numerous ways in which the problem can be resolved. It should not be left to Parliament. In the past six and a half years Parliament has been reluctant to deal with the issue of members' salaries and services. While I do not have that reluctance, I can understand it. We owe the public an explanation of what we are doing and some justification for the level of our salary. I repeat it should be a salary that is defensible but not exorbitant.
We recently gave final approval to a bill which provides for a triennial review of judicial compensation by an advisory panel which will report to the Minister of Justice. Perhaps we should have a similar arrangement for Members of Parliament. In his motion, the hon. member suggests a tribunal of three. I feel there should be more members, but that may not be necessary if they are full time. It would be interesting to see the level of remuneration paid to that tribunal.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 suspect there is nothing more predictable in this place than the view I shall express with regard to the matter being discussed during this private members' hour. The matter before us in the motion presented by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) has to do with the appointment of a tribunal to review salaries of Members of Parliament and various other categories. But I think it is fair to say that most of the discussion by the two members who have spoken thus far has been in defence of higher salaries for Members of Parliament. As I say, I imagine that my view on this is thoroughly predictable, in fact 1 hope it is. I also know it is not exactly a popular view in this place, but I have said many times and still feel that one of the ways we can demonstrate to Canadians that we have come here to serve them is to be much more careful about what we think should be our emoluments, benefits and pensions.
It is easy for us to say that those who criticize our salaries, benefits and pensions are just people who like to criticize or they are jealous, but the fact is that this institution exists to serve the people of Canada and that phrase "the people of Canada" includes millions who are having a tough time; not just the pensioners, widows and veterans on whose behalf 1 speak most often, but many working families, including those where both parents work, and I think in some way we need to demonstrate that we are concerned about them first.
Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, there is something wrong with me, but that is why I came here. It is a story 1 have told on occasion and I may have occasion to tell it again, but not today. I came because I was concerned about what was happening to people. 1 know that 1 speak about the 1930s and early 1940s when I came here, but I have the feeling that every time we get up and defend higher salaries and better benefits for ourselves we widen the gulf between ourselves and the people out there.
As the two hon. members, I am not advocating that we should be at the poverty level or that our salaries should be much lower than they are now, but I do not think it would hurt us to try and establish the proposition that we come here to be of service. I would hate to see the day when the salaries paid here are so attractive that men and women would be encouraged to come here just because it is a good paying job. It would be far better for us to emphasize the proposition that what this place needs is men and women dedicated to the service of their fellow creatures and the well-being of their country, those who are prepared to sacrifice a little bit to render that service.
I find it difficult to use that word because it is not a sacrifice at the level of pay we receive even now, and it goes up by 7 per cent every year. It is not, as one member said, a case of
waiting a long while before there is an adjustment. That used to be so, but for the last several years it has been 7 per cent each January, and to use the comparison made by the hon. member for Edmonton West at that rate our pay will be way up in the stratosphere before long. I plead that we establish the principle that you come to Parliament to be of service, and prepared to work for a little less than you might be able to get somewhere out there.
Mind you, I think that is a bit of a myth. It is so often said that people are working here for a lot less than they could make elsewhere. Well, maybe that applies to some of the lawyers and doctors who are here. I certainly never said that. I have had more pay in this place than I ever had in the jobs I had before coming here, and you can laugh at that because the salaries at that time were nothing compared to salaries today.
I thought it was touching for the hon. member for Edmonton West to be concerned about the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). I respect that office and its occupant but we are paying him something in excess of $80,000 a year, we provide him with a very nice house, everything found, and he makes lots of trips. If the day comes when he retires, and there are people in this country who hope that day is not far away-

Having been a member for at least six years, he has his parliamentary pension; having been Prime Minister for more than four years he will have a prime minister's pension, equivalent to a judge's pension. He will also have his old age security pension and Canada Pension Plan, and all of these pensions will be indexed. Say all you want about that not being much compared to what Ian Sinclair of the CPR can get, or even some of the benefits that may accrue to public servants, but to the Canadians who vote for us that is pretty good.
As for ourselves, some members complain about the level of salaries and so on. However, we should take into consideration all the other things that come our way. I suppose I am more conscious of them because when I came here I could not get something mimeographed unless I got Arthur Beauchesne's signature on it. Telephone calls and the like were not even on the list, and as for travel we had a railway pass good at any time, but we got our out of pocket travelling expenses only twice a year. So we have come a long way. Then there is the help we get with constituency offices, the literature we can send out and one of the best pensions in the country. I know it takes awhile to get it up very far, but as long as you have six years you get the pension for life, no matter what your age may be.
1 suppose this is a debate we may have on some other occasion if a certain proposal comes in, and I do not expect members to agree, they never do, but I want to put the damper on this notion that Members of Parliament are hard done by. Quite frankly, Mr. Speaker, 1 was a little surprised the debate took this turn. When I looked at the motion of the hon. member I assumed we would be debating the creation of a
March 20, 1981

remuneration tribunal in strictly relevant terms. I said to myself: I wonder if I can veer a little bit from that and start talking about our salaries. 1 did not have to; the whole debate has been on that subject. I just want to say, if you will, it is the same old view I have always had. Maybe you can pick holes in it, but I want to put a damper on the idea of higher pay. I would like at least one voice in this place to say to the people out there that I think it is a privilege to serve in this place. You cannot pay us for it.
My hon. friend is quite right in talking about the hours, 14 hours a day, seven days a week, 52 weeks a year. You cannot pay for that. All of us know, too, that there is another price we pay, and that is the difficulties of family life, being away from one's wife and children and so on. The sacrifices made in that area around this place are tremendous. Even if you raise the salary to $100,000 or $200,000 a year, you cannot pay for that.
This brings me back to my feeling that the main purpose in coming here should be to serve the country. I do not want it to be established that you try to get here because it is a good job with good pay, good benefits, and all the rest. Rather, this is the place where people are needed because they are dedicated.
Having used all this time to talk about what is not in the motion, having been prompted to do so by the last two speakers, I should like to say a word about the motion itself. I think the idea of an independent tribunal which would look at all these salaries has merit. However, I attach two conditions to it. First, the recommendations of the tribunal should be subject to parliamentary approval. One or perhaps both hon. members said what they would like to do is get away from raising our own salaries. Mr. Speaker, we cannot divest ourselves of that responsibility. Even if we merely set up a tribunal and never have to pronounce on what it has done, the fact is that we set it up and give it the authority. We will not be able to say in the future, as the children of Israel said to Moses-my knowledge of the Scriptures is becoming somewhat rusty-

He chided them for it, and they said to him, "It is not our fault; we just put in the gold and out came the calf". We cannot divest ourselves of that responsibility. The second condition I would attach to this committee is that the terms of reference for that tribunal should be drawn up very carefully. I do not want it manned or womaned by high-priced judges, high-priced lawyers or high-priced corporate executives, as we have done in the past. I can think of some who have brought down reports that were tremendous. I
Remuneration Tribunal
think there would have to be, on any such tribunal, some pretty good representative Canadians like workers, farmers, school teachers, and maybe even a pensioner or two. On that score I would want more than three members. I think somewhere, in whatever legislation there might be to set up such a tribunal, there have to be words, even if they are words that are in the nature of a preamble, which would remind the tribunal that its purpose is to keep in mind why people come to Parliament, why they become cabinet ministers or judges. The answer to that is that they come to these positions, not to get oodles of money, but to serve the country. I think the rewards for that service, even though it may be tough and you may have to stay at it for years and years, are tremendous; you cannot match that with pay.
I expected just to say 1 support the idea of a tribunal with the two provisos, one that Parliament should be responsible, and two, that it should have the necessary terms of reference, but I am grateful to my colleagues for having made the speeches they did in order that I could express once again the views every member in this House knows I hold.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) I had anticipated we would be speaking about the splendid recommendation of the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert). The problem we have faced around here is not only in dealing with our own salaries but, as the hon. member has -indicated, in coming up with some principle that will guide governments, the tribunal or us in our deliberations about comparability and what is appropriate in the circumstances with respect to salaries.
I have not been here as long as the hon. member for Edmonton West or the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, though a little longer than the hon. member for Northumberland-Miramichi (Mr. Dionne), but it seems to me in the 12 or 13 years I have been around here it has been like trying to grab a handful of fog when trying to determine what would be the appropriate compensation for a Member of Parliament. I know it has been said there are too many lawyers in Parliament, the fact is that the kind of work to be done here requires, in many cases, a certain degree of education or ability to do a specific job. Everyone who comes to the House brings necessary talent or a skill. But if there are so many lawyers and if they form a nucleus, it seems to me that compensation somewhat comparable to that of the legal profession might not be too far out of line.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre says he came here to serve. I think every Member of Parliament can stand in his or her place and say exactly the same. The hon. member said that the cut in pay he took was not really all that great; that, as a matter of fact, he is doing very nicely, thank you. I believe at one stage he was a United Church minister. 1 know how hard my father fought to increase the salaries of United Church ministers because, like everyone else, United Church ministers not only have the opportunity to serve, they also have families to look after and children to put through university. There may be a vicarious thrill for the spouse and children in

March 20, 1981
Remuneration Tribunal
the fact that their husband and father is in the United Church ministry or in the House of Commons, but that does not pay the bills when it comes time for university education or some other kind of necessary training.
We did make financial sacrifices to come here. That is true of many of us who came to this chamber. To try to determine the degree of financial sacrifice we were asked to make or the degree of compensation to be paid to someone who never made that much money before in their life, is extremely difficult. Do we measure it in terms of hours spent, in terms of our dedication, or in terms of the length of time spent here?
One of the great things about the House of Commons and the pay scale here is the fact that all Members of Parliament are paid the same. By that I mean backbench members are all paid the same. We recognize the importance a member on the government side brings to his portfolio or to his job. We say it is equally important that we have a strong and effective opposition. So, very clearly, those particular tasks are the same and should receive comparable compensation.
I like the idea of a tribunal and I think all the questions asked by both the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and the hon. member for Northumberland-Miramichi should be dealt with at committee stage. They were both very careful not to say an MP should get "X" number of dollars a year. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said the compensation should not be too high, and the hon. member for Northumberland-Miramichi said it should not be exorbitant, beyond that which is reasonable. Neither of them put a figure
on it, but somebody has to do that. The responsibility is ours. Surely when a tribunal such as this has to make a decision, it has to go into the background of MPs and what we are required to do. Only in that way can its members come up with a figure which, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said, not only is just but is seen to be just.
1 do not wish to talk this out, Mr. Speaker, because I believe it has considerable merit. The questions which have been asked here are questions which should be asked in the committee, if the recommendation is referred to the committee.
